"She's first-rate, my dear fellow, but not for us," replied Dolokhov.
"I'll tell my sister to invite her to dinner," said Anatole. "Eh?"
"Better wait till she's married..."
"You know, I adore young girls — they lose their heads at once," Anatole went on.
"You've been caught once already by a 'young girl,'" said Dolokhov, who knew about Kuragin's marriage. "Watch out!"
"Well, that can't happen twice! Eh?" said Anatole, with a good-natured laugh.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: The day after the opera the Rostovs went nowhere and nobody came to see them. Marya Dmitrievna talked to the count about something which they kept from Natasha. Natasha guessed they were talking about the old prince and planning something, and this upset and offended her. She was expecting Prince Andrew any moment and twice that day sent a servant to the Vozdvizhenka to find out whether he had arrived. He hadn't. She suffered more now than during her first days in Moscow. To her impatience and longing for him were now added the unpleasant memory of her encounter with Princess Mary and the old prince, and a fear and anxiety whose cause she couldn't understand. She constantly imagined that either he would never come or that something would happen to her before he arrived. She could no longer think of him calmly and steadily as she had before. As soon as she began to think of him, memories of the old prince, of Princess Mary, of the theater, and of Kuragin intruded into her thoughts. The question again arose whether she was not guilty, whether she had not already betrayed Prince Andrew, and again she found herself recalling every tiny detail — every word, every gesture, and every shade of expression on the face of the man who had been able to arouse in her such an incomprehensible and terrifying feeling. To her family, Natasha seemed livelier than usual, but she was far less calm and happy than before.
On Sunday morning Marya Dmitrievna invited her visitors to Mass at her parish church — the Church of the Assumption, built over the graves of plague victims.

"I don't like those fashionable churches," she said, clearly proud of her independence of thought. "God is the same everywhere. We have an excellent priest, he conducts the service properly and with dignity, and the deacon is the same. What holiness is there in turning the choir into a concert? I don't like it — it's just showing off!"

Marya Dmitrievna liked Sundays and knew how to observe them. Her whole house was scrubbed and cleaned on Saturdays; neither she nor the servants worked, and they all wore their best clothes and went to church. At her table there were extra dishes at dinner, and the servants had vodka and roast goose or suckling pig. But in nothing in the house was the holiday so noticeable as in Marya Dmitrievna's broad, stern face, which on that day wore an unchanging look of solemn festivity.

After Mass, when they had finished their coffee in the dining room where the slipcovers had been removed from the furniture, a servant announced that the carriage was ready, and Marya Dmitrievna rose with a stern air. She wore her best shawl, the one she used for paying calls, and announced that she was going to see Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky to have it out with him about Natasha.

After she had gone, a dressmaker from Madame Suppert-Roguet came to see the Rostovs, and Natasha, very glad of this distraction, shut herself in a room next to the drawing room and occupied herself trying on new dresses. Just as she had put on a bodice without sleeves, only loosely basted together, and was turning her head to see in the mirror how the back fit, she heard the lively sounds of her father's voice and another's — a woman's — in the drawing room, which made her blush. It was Helene. Natasha hadn't had time to take off the bodice before the door opened and Countess Bezukhova, dressed in a purple velvet gown with a high collar, came into the room beaming with good-natured, amiable smiles.

"Oh, my enchantress!" she cried to the blushing Natasha. "Charming! No, this is really too much, my dear count," she said to Count Rostov, who had followed her in. "How can you live in Moscow and go nowhere? No, I won't let you off! Mademoiselle George is performing at my house tonight and there'll be some people, and if you don't bring your lovely girls — who are prettier than Mademoiselle George — I won't know you! My husband is away in Tver or I'd send him to fetch you. You must come. You absolutely must! Between eight and nine."

She nodded to the dressmaker, whom she knew and who had curtsied respectfully to her, and settled herself in an armchair near the mirror, draping the folds of her velvet dress attractively. She chatted nonstop, good-naturedly and cheerfully, praising Natasha's beauty all the while. She looked at Natasha's dresses and praised them, as well as a new dress of her own made of "metallic gauze" that she had received from Paris, and advised Natasha to have one like it.
"But anything suits you, my darling!" she remarked.

A smile of pleasure never left Natasha's face. She felt happy and as if she were blossoming under the praise of this dear Countess Bezukhova, who had formerly seemed to her so unapproachable and important and was now so kind to her. Natasha brightened up and felt almost in love with this woman who was so beautiful and so kind. Helene, for her part, was genuinely delighted with Natasha and wanted to give her a good time. Anatole had asked her to bring him and Natasha together, and she was visiting the Rostovs for that purpose. The idea of throwing her brother and Natasha together amused her.

Though at one time, in Petersburg, she had been annoyed with Natasha for drawing Boris away, she didn't think of that now, and in her own way genuinely wished Natasha well. As she was leaving the Rostovs, she called her new friend aside.
"My brother dined with me yesterday — we nearly died of laughter — he ate nothing and kept sighing about you, my darling! He is madly, quite madly, in love with you, my dear."
Natasha blushed scarlet when she heard this.

"How she blushes, how she blushes, my pretty!" said Helene. "You must certainly come. If you love somebody, my darling, that's no reason to shut yourself away. Even if you are engaged, I'm sure your fiance would wish you to go into society rather than be bored to death."

"So she knows I'm engaged, and she and her husband Pierre — that good Pierre — have talked and laughed about this. So it's all fine." And again, under Helene's influence, what had seemed terrible now seemed simple and natural. "And she is such a great lady, so kind, and she obviously likes me so much. And why not enjoy myself?" thought Natasha, gazing at Helene with wide, wondering eyes.

Marya Dmitrievna came back to dinner silent and serious, having clearly suffered a defeat at the old prince's. She was still too agitated by the encounter to be able to talk about it calmly. In answer to the count's questions she replied that things were all right and that she would tell about it the next day. On hearing of Countess Bezukhova's visit and the invitation for that evening, Marya Dmitrievna remarked:
"I don't care to have anything to do with Bezukhova and don't advise you to either; however, if you've promised — go. It will take your mind off things," she added, addressing Natasha.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: Count Rostov took the girls to Countess Bezukhova's. There were a good many people there, but nearly all strangers to Natasha. Count Rostov was displeased to see that the company consisted almost entirely of men and women known for the looseness of their behavior. Mademoiselle George was standing in a corner of the drawing room surrounded by young men. There were several Frenchmen present, among them Metivier, who from the time Helene reached Moscow had been a regular in her house. The count decided not to sit down to cards or let his girls out of his sight and to leave as soon as Mademoiselle George's performance was over.

Anatole was at the door, obviously on the lookout for the Rostovs. Immediately after greeting the count, he went up to Natasha and followed her. As soon as she saw him she was seized by the same feeling she had had at the opera — a gratified vanity at his admiration and fear at the absence of any moral barrier between them.

Helene welcomed Natasha with delight and was loud in her admiration of her beauty and her dress. Soon after their arrival, Mademoiselle George went out to change her costume. In the drawing room people began arranging chairs and taking their seats. Anatole moved a chair for Natasha and was about to sit down beside her, but the count, who never lost sight of her, took the seat himself. Anatole sat down behind her.
Mademoiselle George, with her bare, plump, dimpled arms and a red shawl draped over one shoulder, came into the space left for her and struck an unnatural pose. Enthusiastic whispering was audible.

Mademoiselle George looked sternly and gloomily at the audience and began reciting some French verses describing her guilty love for her son. In some places she raised her voice, in others she whispered, lifting her head triumphantly; sometimes she paused and uttered hoarse sounds, rolling her eyes.
"Adorable! Divine! Delicious!" was heard from every side.

Natasha looked at the plump actress, but neither saw nor heard nor understood anything of what was going on before her. She only felt herself once again completely carried away into this strange, senseless world — so far removed from her old life — a world in which it was impossible to tell what was good or bad, reasonable or senseless. Behind her sat Anatole, and conscious of his nearness she felt a frightened sense of anticipation.
After the first monologue the whole company rose and surrounded Mademoiselle George, expressing their enthusiasm.
"How beautiful she is!" Natasha remarked to her father, who had also gotten up and was moving through the crowd toward the actress.
"I don't think so when I look at you!" said Anatole, following Natasha. He said this at a moment when only she could hear him. "You are enchanting... from the moment I saw you I have never ceased..."

"Come, come, Natasha!" said the count, turning back for his daughter. "How beautiful she is!" Natasha, without saying anything, stepped up to her father and looked at him with surprised, questioning eyes.
After giving several recitations, Mademoiselle George left, and Countess Bezukhova invited her guests into the ballroom.

The count wanted to go home, but Helene begged him not to spoil her impromptu ball, and the Rostovs stayed. Anatole asked Natasha for a waltz, and as they danced he pressed her waist and hand and told her she was bewitching and that he loved her. During the ecossaise, which she also danced with him, Anatole said nothing when they happened to be alone, but simply gazed at her. Natasha lifted her frightened eyes to him, but there was such confident tenderness in his affectionate look and smile that she could not, while looking at him, say what she needed to say. She lowered her eyes.
"Don't say such things to me. I'm engaged and I love another," she said quickly... She glanced at him.
Anatole was not upset or hurt by what she had said.
"Don't talk to me about that! What can I do?" said he. "I tell you I'm madly, madly, in love with you! Is it my fault that you are enchanting?... It's our turn to begin."

Natasha, excited and bewildered, looked around with wide, frightened eyes and seemed merrier than usual. She understood hardly anything that went on that evening. They danced the ecossaise and the Grossvater. Her father asked her to come home, but she begged to stay. Wherever she went and whomever she was talking to, she felt his eyes upon her. Later she recalled how she had asked her father to let her go to the dressing room to fix her dress, that Helene had followed her and spoken laughingly of her brother's love, and that she met Anatole again in the small sitting room. Helene had disappeared, leaving them alone, and Anatole had taken her hand and said in a tender voice:
"I cannot come to visit you, but is it possible that I shall never see you? I love you madly. Can I never...?" and, blocking her path, he brought his face close to hers.
His large, glittering, masculine eyes were so close to hers that she saw nothing but them.
"Natalie?" he whispered questioningly while she felt her hands being painfully squeezed. "Natalie?"
"I don't understand. I have nothing to say," her eyes replied.

Burning lips were pressed to hers, and at the same instant she felt herself released, and Helene's footsteps and the rustle of her dress were heard in the room. Natasha looked around at her, and then, red and trembling, threw a frightened look of inquiry at Anatole and moved toward the door.
"One word, just one, for God's sake!" cried Anatole.
She paused. She so needed a word from him that would explain what had happened and to which she could find no answer.
"Natalie, just a word, only one!" he kept repeating, clearly not knowing what to say, and he repeated it until Helene came up to them.
Helene returned with Natasha to the drawing room. The Rostovs left without staying for supper.

After reaching home, Natasha did not sleep all night. She was tormented by the unanswerable question of whether she loved Anatole or Prince Andrew. She loved Prince Andrew — she remembered distinctly how deeply she loved him. But she also loved Anatole — of that there was no doubt. "Otherwise, how could all this have happened?" she thought. "If, after that, I could return his smile when saying goodbye, if I was able to let it come to that, it means I loved him from the first. It means he is kind, noble, and wonderful, and I couldn't help loving him. What am I to do if I love him and the other one too?" she asked herself, unable to find an answer to these terrible questions.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: Morning came with its cares and bustle. Everyone got up and began to move about and talk, dressmakers came again. Marya Dmitrievna appeared, and they were called to breakfast. Natasha kept looking uneasily at everybody with wide-open eyes, as if trying to intercept every glance directed at her, and tried to appear the same as usual.
After breakfast, which was her best time, Marya Dmitrievna settled into her armchair and called Natasha and the count over.

"Well, friends, I've now thought the whole matter over and this is my advice," she began. "Yesterday, as you know, I went to see Prince Bolkonsky. Well, I had a talk with him... He got it into his head to start shouting, but I'm not one to be shouted down. I said what I had to say!"
"Well, and he?" asked the count.

"He? He's out of his mind... he wouldn't listen. But what's the use of talking? As it is, we've worn the poor girl out," said Marya Dmitrievna. "My advice to you is: finish your business and go back home to Otradnoe... and wait there."
"Oh, no!" exclaimed Natasha.
"Yes, go back," said Marya Dmitrievna, "and wait there. If your fiance comes here now there'll be no avoiding a quarrel; but alone with the old man he'll talk things over and then come on to you."

Count Rostov approved of this suggestion, seeing its good sense. If the old man came around, it would be even better to visit him in Moscow or at Bald Hills later; and if not, the wedding, against his wishes, could only be arranged at Otradnoe.
"That's exactly right. And I'm sorry I went to see him and took her," said the old count.

"No, why be sorry? Being here, you had to pay your respects. But if he won't — that's his business," said Marya Dmitrievna, looking for something in her handbag. "Besides, the trousseau is ready, so there's nothing to wait for; and what's not ready I'll send after you. Though I don't like letting you go, it's the best thing. So go, with God's blessing!"
Having found what she was looking for in the handbag, she handed it to Natasha. It was a letter from Princess Mary.
"She's written to you. How she torments herself, poor thing! She's afraid you might think she doesn't like you."
"But she doesn't like me," said Natasha.
"Don't talk nonsense!" cried Marya Dmitrievna.

"I won't believe anyone — I know she doesn't like me," replied Natasha boldly as she took the letter, and her face expressed a cold and angry determination that caused Marya Dmitrievna to look at her more closely and frown.
"Don't answer like that, my good girl!" she said. "What I say is true! Write an answer!"
Natasha didn't reply and went to her own room to read Princess Mary's letter.

Princess Mary wrote that she was in despair at the misunderstanding between them. Whatever her father's feelings might be, she begged Natasha to believe that she could not help loving her as the one chosen by her brother, for whose happiness she was ready to sacrifice everything.

"Do not think, however," she wrote, "that my father is ill-disposed toward you. He is an invalid and an old man who must be forgiven; but he is good and generous and will love the woman who makes his son happy." Princess Mary went on to ask Natasha to set a time when she could see her again.

After reading the letter, Natasha sat down at the writing table to answer it. "Dear Princess," she wrote quickly and mechanically in French, and then paused. What more could she write after everything that had happened the evening before? "Yes, yes! All that has happened, and now everything is changed," she thought as she sat with the unfinished letter before her. "Must I break off with him? Must I really? That's awful..." and to escape from these dreadful thoughts she went to Sonya and began sorting patterns with her.

After dinner Natasha went to her room and again took up Princess Mary's letter. "Can it really be all over?" she thought. "Can it be that all this has happened so quickly and has destroyed everything that went before?" She recalled her love for Prince Andrew in all its former strength, and at the same time felt that she loved Kuragin. She vividly pictured herself as Prince Andrew's wife, and the scenes of happiness with him she had imagined so often, and at the same time, glowing with excitement, recalled every detail of yesterday's encounter with Anatole.

"Why couldn't that be as well?" she sometimes asked herself in complete bewilderment. "Only that way could I be completely happy; but now I have to choose, and I can't be happy without either of them. Only," she thought, "to tell Prince Andrew what has happened or to hide it from him are both equally impossible. But with that one nothing is ruined. But am I really to give up forever the joy of Prince Andrew's love, in which I've lived so long?"
"Please, Miss!" whispered a maid, entering the room with a mysterious air. "A man told me to give you this—" and she handed Natasha a letter.

"Only, for Christ's sake..." the girl went on, as Natasha, without thinking, mechanically broke the seal and read a love letter from Anatole, of which, without taking in a word, she understood only that it was a letter from him — from the man she loved. Yes, she loved him, or else how could what had happened have happened? And how could she have a love letter from him in her hand?
With trembling hands Natasha held that passionate love letter which Dolokhov had composed for Anatole, and as she read it she found in it an echo of everything she imagined she herself was feeling.

"Since yesterday evening my fate has been sealed; to be loved by you or to die. There is no other way for me," the letter began. Then he went on to say that he knew her parents would not give her to him — for this there were secret reasons he could reveal only to her — but that if she loved him she need only say the word yes, and no human power could prevent their happiness. Love would conquer all. He would steal her away and carry her off to the ends of the earth.
"Yes, yes! I love him!" thought Natasha, reading the letter for the twentieth time and finding some especially deep meaning in each word of it.
That evening Marya Dmitrievna was going to the Akharovs' and proposed to take the girls with her. Natasha, pleading a headache, stayed home.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Returning late in the evening, Sonya went to Natasha's room and to her surprise found her still dressed and asleep on the sofa. Anatole's letter lay open on the table beside her. Sonya picked it up and read it.

As she read, she glanced at the sleeping Natasha, trying to find in her face an explanation of what she was reading, but didn't find it. Her face was calm, gentle, and happy. Clutching her chest to keep from choking, Sonya, pale and trembling with fear and agitation, sat down in an armchair and burst into tears.

"How was it I noticed nothing? How could it go so far? Can she have stopped loving Prince Andrew? And how could she let Kuragin go to such lengths? He's a deceiver and a villain, that's plain! What will Nicholas — dear, noble Nicholas — do when he hears of it? So this is the meaning of her excited, determined, unnatural look the day before yesterday, yesterday, and today," thought Sonya. "But it can't be that she loves him! She probably opened the letter without knowing who it was from. Probably she's offended by it. She couldn't do such a thing!"
Sonya wiped away her tears and went up to Natasha, studying her face again.
"Natasha!" she said, barely audibly.
Natasha woke and saw Sonya.
"Ah, you're back?"
And with the openness and tenderness that often come at the moment of waking, she embraced her friend, but noticing Sonya's look of distress, her own face expressed confusion and suspicion.
"Sonya, you've read that letter?" she demanded.
"Yes," answered Sonya softly.
Natasha smiled rapturously.
"No, Sonya, I can't hold it in any longer!" she said. "I can't hide it from you any longer. You know, we love each other! Sonya, darling, he writes... Sonya..."
Sonya stared open-eyed at Natasha, unable to believe her ears.
"And Bolkonsky?" she asked.
"Oh, Sonya, if you only knew how happy I am!" cried Natasha. "You don't know what love is..."
"But, Natasha, can that really be all over?"
Natasha looked at Sonya with wide-open eyes as if she couldn't grasp the question.
"Well, then, are you refusing Prince Andrew?" said Sonya.
"Oh, you don't understand anything! Don't talk nonsense, just listen!" said Natasha with momentary annoyance.

"But I can't believe it," insisted Sonya. "I don't understand. How is it you've loved a man for a whole year and suddenly... Why, you've only seen him three times! Natasha, I don't believe you — you're joking! In three days to forget everything and just..."

"Three days?" said Natasha. "It seems to me I've loved him a hundred years. It seems to me that I've never loved anyone before. You can't understand it... Sonya, wait a bit, sit here," and Natasha embraced and kissed her.

"I'd heard that it happens like this, and you must have heard it too, but it's only now that I feel such love. It's not the same as before. As soon as I saw him I felt he was my master and I his slave, and that I couldn't help loving him. Yes, his slave! Whatever he commands I'll do. You don't understand that. What can I do? What can I do, Sonya?" cried Natasha with a happy yet frightened expression.
"But think what you're doing," cried Sonya. "I can't let this go on. This secret correspondence... How could you let him go so far?" she went on, with a horror and disgust she could hardly conceal.
"I told you that I have no will," Natasha replied. "Why can't you understand? I love him!"
"Then I won't let it come to that... I'll tell!" cried Sonya, bursting into tears.
"What do you mean? For God's sake... If you tell, you are my enemy!" declared Natasha. "You want me to be miserable, you want us to be separated..."
When she saw Natasha's fright, Sonya shed tears of shame and pity for her friend.
"But what has happened between you?" she asked. "What has he said to you? Why doesn't he come to the house?"
Natasha didn't answer her questions.
"For God's sake, Sonya, don't tell anyone, don't torture me," Natasha begged. "Remember, no one should interfere in such matters! I've confided in you..."

"But why all this secrecy? Why doesn't he come to the house?" asked Sonya. "Why doesn't he openly ask for your hand? You know Prince Andrew gave you complete freedom — if this is really happening. But I don't believe it! Natasha, have you considered what these secret reasons could be?"
Natasha looked at Sonya with astonishment. Evidently this question had never occurred to her, and she didn't know how to answer it.
"I don't know what the reasons are. But there must be reasons!"
Sonya sighed and shook her head doubtfully.
"If there were reasons..." she began.
But Natasha, guessing her doubts, interrupted her in alarm.
"Sonya, you can't doubt him! You can't, you can't! Don't you understand?" she cried.
"Does he love you?"
"Does he love me?" Natasha repeated with a smile of pity at her friend's lack of understanding. "Why, you've read his letter and you've seen him."
"But if he's dishonorable?"
"He! Dishonorable? If you only knew!" exclaimed Natasha.
"If he's an honorable man, he should either declare his intentions or stop seeing you; and if you won't do this, I will. I'll write to him, and I'll tell Papa!" said Sonya firmly.
"But I can't live without him!" cried Natasha.
"Natasha, I don't understand you. And what are you saying! Think of your father and of Nicholas."

"I don't want anyone, I don't love anyone but him. How dare you say he's dishonorable? Don't you know that I love him?" screamed Natasha. "Go away, Sonya! I don't want to quarrel with you, but go, for God's sake, go! You see how I'm suffering!" Natasha cried angrily, in a voice of despair and suppressed fury. Sonya burst into sobs and ran from the room.

Natasha went to the table and without a moment's reflection wrote the answer to Princess Mary which she had been unable to write all morning. In this letter she said briefly that all their misunderstandings were over; that making use of the generosity of Prince Andrew, who when he went abroad had given her her freedom, she begged Princess Mary to forget everything and forgive her if she had been at fault toward her, but that she could not be his wife. At that moment, all of this seemed perfectly easy, simple, and clear to Natasha.
On Friday the Rostovs were to return to the country, but on Wednesday the count went with the prospective buyer to his estate near Moscow.

On the day the count left, Sonya and Natasha were invited to a big dinner party at the Kargins', and Marya Dmitrievna took them there. At the party Natasha again met Anatole, and Sonya noticed that she spoke to him, trying not to be overheard, and that all through dinner she was more agitated than ever. When they got home, Natasha was the first to begin the explanation Sonya expected.
"There, Sonya, you were saying all sorts of nonsense about him," Natasha began in a gentle voice such as children use when they want to be praised. "We had an explanation today."
"Well, what happened? What did he say? Natasha, how glad I am you're not angry with me! Tell me everything — the whole truth. What did he say?"
Natasha became thoughtful.
"Oh, Sonya, if you knew him as I do! He said... He asked me what I had promised Bolkonsky. He was glad I was free to refuse him."
Sonya sighed sadly.
"But you haven't refused Bolkonsky?" said she.
"Perhaps I have. Perhaps it's all over between me and Bolkonsky. Why do you think so badly of me?"
"I don't think anything, only I don't understand this..."

"Wait a bit, Sonya, you'll understand everything. You'll see what kind of man he is! Now don't think badly of me or of him. I don't think badly of anyone: I love and pity everybody. But what am I to do?"
Sonya was not won over by the tender tone Natasha used with her. The more emotional and pleading Natasha's face became, the more serious and stern Sonya's grew.
"Natasha," said she, "you asked me not to speak to you, and I haven't spoken, but now you yourself have begun. I don't trust him, Natasha. Why all this secrecy?"
"Again, again!" interrupted Natasha.
"Natasha, I'm afraid for you!"
"Afraid of what?"
"I'm afraid you're heading for disaster," said Sonya firmly, and was herself horrified at what she had said.
Anger again showed in Natasha's face.
"Then I'll go to my ruin, I will, as soon as possible! It's none of your business! It won't be you but I who'll suffer. Leave me alone, leave me alone! I hate you!"
"Natasha!" moaned Sonya, aghast.
"I hate you, I hate you! You're my enemy forever!" And Natasha ran out of the room.

Natasha didn't speak to Sonya again and avoided her. With the same expression of agitated surprise and guilt she went about the house, picking up first one activity, then another, and immediately dropping them.
Hard as it was for Sonya, she watched her friend and wouldn't let her out of her sight.

The day before the count was due to return, Sonya noticed that Natasha sat by the drawing room window all morning as if expecting something, and that she made a signal to an officer who drove past — whom Sonya took to be Anatole.

Sonya began watching her friend still more closely and noticed that at dinner and all that evening Natasha was in a strange and unnatural state. She answered questions at random, began sentences she didn't finish, and laughed at everything.
After tea Sonya noticed a maid at Natasha's door, timidly waiting to let her pass. She let the girl go in, and then, listening at the door, learned that another letter had been delivered.
Then suddenly it became clear to Sonya that Natasha had some terrible plan for that evening. Sonya knocked at her door. Natasha wouldn't let her in.

"She will run away with him!" thought Sonya. "She's capable of anything. There was something especially desperate and determined in her face today. She cried as she said goodbye to Uncle," Sonya remembered. "Yes, that's it — she means to elope with him. But what am I to do?" she thought, recalling all the signs that clearly indicated Natasha had some terrible intention. "The count is away. What am I to do? Write to Kuragin demanding an explanation? But what obliges him to reply? Write to Pierre, as Prince Andrew asked me to in case of some misfortune?... But perhaps she really has already refused Bolkonsky — she sent a letter to Princess Mary yesterday. And Uncle is away..." To tell Marya Dmitrievna, who had such faith in Natasha, seemed terrible to Sonya. "Well, anyway," thought Sonya as she stood in the dark corridor, "now or never I must prove that I remember the family's goodness to me and that I love Nicholas. Yes! If I don't sleep for three nights I won't leave this corridor, and I will hold her back by force and not let the family be disgraced," she thought.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Anatole had recently moved in with Dolokhov. The plan for Natasha Rostova's abduction had been arranged and the preparations made by Dolokhov a few days before, and on the day that Sonya, after listening at Natasha's door, resolved to protect her, the plan was supposed to be carried out. Natasha had promised to come out to Kuragin at the back porch at ten that evening. Kuragin was to put her in a troika he would have ready and drive her forty miles to the village of Kamenka, where a defrocked priest was standing by to perform a marriage ceremony. At Kamenka a fresh set of horses was to wait, which would take them to the Warsaw highway, and from there they would flee abroad with post horses.
Anatole had a passport, an order for post horses, ten thousand rubles he had taken from his sister, and another ten thousand borrowed with Dolokhov's help.

Two witnesses for the sham marriage — Khvostikov, a retired petty official whom Dolokhov used in his gambling dealings, and Makarin, a retired hussar, a kindly, weak fellow who had an unlimited affection for Kuragin — were sitting at tea in Dolokhov's front room.

In his large study, the walls hung to the ceiling with Persian rugs, bearskins, and weapons, Dolokhov sat in a traveling cloak and high boots at an open desk on which lay an abacus and some bundles of paper money. Anatole, with his uniform unbuttoned, paced back and forth from the room where the witnesses were sitting, through the study, to the room behind where his French valet and others were packing the last of his things. Dolokhov was counting money and jotting down figures.
"Well," he said, "Khvostikov must have two thousand."
"Give it to him, then," said Anatole.
"Makarka" (their nickname for Makarin) "will go through fire and water for you for nothing. So here are our accounts all settled," said Dolokhov, showing him the figures. "Is that right?"
"Yes, of course," returned Anatole, clearly not listening to Dolokhov and looking straight ahead with a smile that never left his face.
Dolokhov slammed down the lid of his desk and turned to Anatole with an ironic smile:
"You know what? You'd really better drop the whole thing. There's still time!"
"Idiot," retorted Anatole. "Don't talk nonsense! If you only knew... it's the devil knows what!"
"No, really, give it up!" said Dolokhov. "I'm speaking seriously. It's no joke, this scheme you've cooked up."
"What, teasing again? Go to the devil! Eh?" said Anatole, making a face. "Really, it's no time for your stupid jokes," and he left the room.
Dolokhov smiled contemptuously and condescendingly when Anatole had gone out.
"Wait a moment," he called after him. "I'm not joking — I'm talking seriously. Come here, come here!"
Anatole returned and looked at Dolokhov, trying to pay attention and clearly submitting to him involuntarily.

"Now listen. I'm telling you this for the last time. Why would I joke about it? Did I stand in your way? Who arranged everything for you? Who found the priest and got the passport? Who raised the money? I did all of it."
"Well, thank you for it. Do you think I'm not grateful?" And Anatole sighed and embraced Dolokhov.

"I helped you, but all the same I must tell you the truth: it's a dangerous business, and if you think about it — a stupid one. Well, you'll carry her off — fine! Will they let it end there? It'll come out that you're already married. They'll have you up in criminal court..."

"Oh, nonsense, nonsense!" Anatole exclaimed, making a face again. "Didn't I explain to you? What?" And Anatole, with the fondness dull-witted people have for any conclusion they've reached by their own reasoning, repeated the argument he had already put to Dolokhov a hundred times. "Didn't I explain that I've come to this conclusion: if this marriage is invalid" — he crooked one finger — "then I have nothing to answer for; but if it is valid, no matter! Abroad no one will know anything about it. Isn't that so? And don't lecture me, don't, don't."
"Seriously, you'd better drop it! You'll only get yourself into a mess!"

"Go to the devil!" cried Anatole, and clutching his hair, left the room. But he came back at once and dropped into an armchair in front of Dolokhov with his legs tucked under him. "It's maddening! Here, feel how my heart's pounding!" He took Dolokhov's hand and put it on his chest. "What a foot, my dear fellow! What a look! A goddess!" he added in French. "What?"
Dolokhov, with a cold smile and a gleam in his handsome, insolent eyes, looked at him — clearly wanting to get some more entertainment out of him.
"Well, and when the money's gone, what then?"
"What then? Eh?" repeated Anatole, genuinely confused by a thought of the future. "What then?... Then, I don't know... But why talk nonsense!" He glanced at his watch. "It's time!"
Anatole went into the back room.
"Now then! Nearly ready? You're dawdling!" he shouted to the servants.
Dolokhov put away the money, called a footman whom he ordered to bring something for them to eat and drink before the journey, and went into the room where Khvostikov and Makarin were sitting.
Anatole lay on the sofa in the study, leaning on his elbow and smiling pensively, while his handsome lips murmured tenderly to himself.
"Come and eat something. Have a drink!" Dolokhov shouted to him from the other room.
"I don't want to," answered Anatole, still smiling.
"Come on! Balaga is here."

Anatole got up and went into the dining room. Balaga was a famous troika driver who had known Dolokhov and Anatole for some six years and had served them well. More than once, when Anatole's regiment was stationed at Tver, he had taken him from Tver in the evening, brought him to Moscow by daybreak, and driven him back the next night. More than once he had helped Dolokhov escape when pursued. More than once he had driven them through town with gypsies and women of pleasure. More than once in their service he had run over pedestrians and overturned vehicles in the streets of Moscow and had always been protected from the consequences by "my gentlemen," as he called them. He had ruined more than one horse in their service. More than once they had beaten him, and more than once they had gotten him drunk on champagne and Madeira, which he loved. And he knew more than one thing about each of them that would long ago have sent an ordinary man to Siberia. They often invited Balaga to their wild parties and made him drink and dance with the gypsies, and more than a thousand rubles of their money had passed through his hands. In their service he risked his skin and his life twenty times a year, and had lost more horses than the money he got from them would buy. But he liked them; liked that insane driving at twelve miles an hour, liked overturning a driver or running down a pedestrian, and flying at full gallop through Moscow's streets. He liked hearing those wild, drunken shouts behind him: "Faster! Faster!" when it was impossible to go any faster. He liked giving a cruel lash across the neck to some peasant who, more dead than alive, was already scrambling out of his way. "Real gentlemen!" he considered them.

Anatole and Dolokhov liked Balaga too, for his masterful driving and because he liked the same things they liked. With others Balaga bargained, charging twenty-five rubles for a two-hour drive, and rarely drove himself, usually leaving it to his young men. But with "his gentlemen" he always drove himself and never asked for payment. Only a couple of times a year — when he learned from their valets that they had money on hand — he would turn up of a morning, completely sober, and with a deep bow would ask them for help. The gentlemen always made him sit down.
"Do help me out, Theodore Ivanich, sir," or "your excellency," he would say. "I'm completely out of horses. Let me have what you can to go to the horse fair."
And Anatole and Dolokhov, when they had money, would give him a thousand or a couple of thousand rubles.

Balaga was a fair-haired, short, snub-nosed peasant of about twenty-seven; red-faced, with a particularly red, thick neck, glittering little eyes, and a small beard. He wore a fine, dark blue, silk-lined cloth coat over a sheepskin.
On entering the room he crossed himself, facing the icon corner, and went up to Dolokhov, holding out a small, dark hand.
"Theodore Ivanich!" he said, bowing.
"Hello, friend! Well, here he is!"
"Good day, your excellency!" he said, again holding out his hand to Anatole, who had just come in.
"I say, Balaga," said Anatole, putting his hands on the man's shoulders, "do you care for me or not? Eh? Now, do me a service... What horses have you brought? Eh?"
"As your messenger ordered — your special beasts," replied Balaga.
"Well, listen, Balaga! Drive all three to death but get me there in three hours. Eh?"
"When they're dead, what will I drive?" said Balaga with a wink.
"Mind, I'll smash your face! Don't joke!" cried Anatole, suddenly rolling his eyes.
"Why would I joke?" said the driver, laughing. "As if I'd begrudge my gentlemen anything! As fast as the horses can gallop, that's how fast we'll go!"
"Ah!" said Anatole. "Well, sit down."
"Yes, sit down!" said Dolokhov.
"I'll stand, Theodore Ivanich."
"Sit down; nonsense! Have a drink!" said Anatole, and filled a large glass of Madeira for him.
The driver's eyes sparkled at the sight of the wine. After refusing it for propriety's sake, he drank it and wiped his mouth with a red silk handkerchief he took from his cap.
"And when are we to start, your excellency?"
"Well..." Anatole looked at his watch. "We'll start at once. Mind, Balaga! You'll get there in time? Eh?"
"That depends on our luck in starting — otherwise, why shouldn't we be there in time?" replied Balaga. "Didn't we get you to Tver in seven hours? I think you remember that, your excellency?"

"Do you know, one Christmas I drove from Tver," said Anatole, smiling at the memory and turning to Makarin, who gazed at him with adoring, wide-open eyes. "Will you believe it, Makarka, it took your breath away, the speed we flew. We came across a line of loaded sleighs and drove right over two of them. Eh?"

"Those were horses!" Balaga continued the story. "That time I'd harnessed two young side horses with the bay in the shafts," he went on, turning to Dolokhov. "Will you believe it, Theodore Ivanich, those animals flew forty miles? I couldn't hold them in — my hands went numb in the bitter cold so that I dropped the reins. 'Catch hold yourself, your excellency!' says I, and I just tumbled to the bottom of the sleigh and sprawled there. It wasn't a case of urging them on — there was no holding them back till we reached the place. The devils got us there in three hours! Only the one on the near side died of it."

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Anatole went out of the room and returned a few minutes later wearing a fur coat belted with silver and a sable cap jauntily set to one side, very becoming to his handsome face. Having looked in a mirror and taken up the same pose he had struck before it, he raised a glass of wine.

"Well, goodbye, Theodore. Thank you for everything, and farewell!" said Anatole. "Well, comrades and friends..." he paused a moment "... of my youth, farewell!" he said, turning to Makarin and the others.

Though they were all going with him, Anatole clearly wanted to make something touching and solemn out of this address to his companions. He spoke slowly in a loud voice, throwing out his chest and slightly swaying one leg.

"All take glasses; you too, Balaga. Well, comrades and friends of my youth, we've had our fun, lived and reveled. Eh? And now, when shall we meet again? I'm going abroad. We've had a great time — now farewell, lads! To our health! Hurrah!..." he cried, and draining his glass flung it on the floor.
"To your health!" said Balaga, who also drained his glass and wiped his mouth with his handkerchief.
Makarin embraced Anatole with tears in his eyes.
"Ah, Prince, how sorry I am to part from you!"
"Let's go. Let's go!" cried Anatole.
Balaga was about to leave the room.
"No, stop!" said Anatole. "Shut the door; we have to sit down first. That's the custom."
They shut the door and all sat down.
"Now, quick march, lads!" said Anatole, rising.
Joseph, his valet, handed him his saber pouch and sword, and they all went out into the vestibule.

"And where's the fur cloak?" asked Dolokhov. "Hey, Ignatka! Go to Matrena Matrevna and ask her for the sable cloak. I know how elopements go," Dolokhov continued with a wink. "She'll rush out half dead with fright, just in whatever she's wearing; if you delay at all there'll be tears and 'Papa' and 'Mama,' and she'll freeze in a minute and have to go back. But you wrap the fur cloak around her right away and carry her to the sleigh."
The valet brought a woman's fox-lined cloak.
"Fool, I told you the sable one! Hey, Matrena, the sable!" he shouted so that his voice rang through the rooms.
A handsome, slim, pale-faced gypsy girl with glittering black eyes and curly blue-black hair, wearing a red shawl, ran out with a sable mantle on her arm.
"Here, I don't grudge it — take it!" she said, obviously afraid of her master and yet reluctant to give up her cloak.
Dolokhov, without answering, took the cloak, threw it over Matrena, and wrapped her up in it.

"That's how you do it," said Dolokhov, "and then like this!" and he turned the collar up around her head, leaving only a little of her face uncovered. "And then like this, see?" and he pushed Anatole's head forward to meet the gap left by the collar, through which Matrena's brilliant smile was visible.
"Well, goodbye, Matrena," said Anatole, kissing her. "Ah, my good times here are over. Remember me to Steshka. There, goodbye! Goodbye, Matrena — wish me luck!"
"Well, Prince, may God give you great luck!" said Matrena in her gypsy accent.

Two troikas were standing before the porch, and two young drivers were holding the horses. Balaga took his seat in the front one, and holding his elbows high, carefully arranged the reins. Anatole and Dolokhov got in with him. Makarin, Khvostikov, and a valet took their seats in the other sleigh.
"Well, are you ready?" asked Balaga.
"Go!" he cried, twisting the reins around his hands, and the troika tore down the Nikitsky Boulevard.

"Whoa! Get out of the way! Hey!... Whoa!" The shouting of Balaga and the sturdy young fellow on the box was all that could be heard. On Arbat Square the troika collided with a carriage; something cracked, shouts rang out, and the troika flew along Arbat Street.
After racing along the Podnovinsky Boulevard, Balaga began to rein in and, turning back, drew up at the crossing of the old Konyusheny Street.

The young fellow on the box jumped down to hold the horses, and Anatole and Dolokhov went along the sidewalk. When they reached the gate, Dolokhov whistled. The whistle was answered, and a maid ran out.
"Come into the courtyard or you'll be seen; she'll come out right away," said she.
Dolokhov stayed by the gate. Anatole followed the maid into the courtyard, turned the corner, and ran up to the porch.
He was met by Gabriel, Marya Dmitrievna's enormous footman.
"Come to the mistress, please," said the footman in his deep bass, blocking any retreat.
"To what mistress? Who are you?" asked Anatole in a breathless whisper.
"Kindly step in. My orders are to bring you in."
"Kuragin! Come back!" shouted Dolokhov. "Betrayed! Back!"

Dolokhov, after Anatole entered, had stayed at the wicket gate and was struggling with the yard porter who was trying to lock it. With a last desperate effort, Dolokhov pushed the porter aside, and when Anatole ran back, seized him by the arm, pulled him through the wicket, and ran back with him to the troika.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: Marya Dmitrievna, having found Sonya weeping in the corridor, made her confess everything, and intercepting the note to Natasha, she read it and went into Natasha's room with it in her hand.
"You shameless good-for-nothing!" said she. "I won't hear a word."

Pushing back Natasha, who looked at her with astonished but tearless eyes, she locked her in; and having ordered the yard porter to admit the persons who would be coming that evening but not to let them out again, and having told the footman to bring them up to her, she settled herself in the drawing room to wait for the abductors.

When Gabriel came to inform her that the men who had come had run away again, she rose frowning, and clasping her hands behind her paced through the rooms for a long time considering what she should do. Toward midnight she went to Natasha's room, fingering the key in her pocket. Sonya was sitting sobbing in the corridor. "Marya Dmitrievna, for God's sake let me in to her!" she begged, but Marya Dmitrievna unlocked the door and went in without answering... "Disgusting, abominable... In my house... horrid girl, hussy! I'm only sorry for her father!" she thought, trying to contain her fury. "Hard as it may be, I'll tell them all to hold their tongues and will hide it from the count." She entered the room with resolute steps. Natasha was lying on the sofa, her head hidden in her hands, and she didn't stir. She was in exactly the same position in which Marya Dmitrievna had left her.

"A nice girl! Very nice!" said Marya Dmitrievna. "Arranging meetings with lovers in my house! It's no use pretending — listen when I'm speaking to you!" And Marya Dmitrievna touched her arm. "Listen when I speak! You've disgraced yourself like the lowest of hussies. I'd treat you differently, but I'm sorry for your father, so I'll cover it up."
Natasha didn't change her position, but her whole body heaved with noiseless, convulsive sobs that choked her. Marya Dmitrievna glanced around at Sonya and sat down on the sofa beside Natasha.
"It's lucky for him that he escaped me; but I'll find him!" she said in her rough voice. "Do you hear what I'm saying or not?" she added.

She put her large hand under Natasha's face and turned it toward her. Both Marya Dmitrievna and Sonya were amazed at how Natasha looked. Her eyes were dry and glistening, her lips compressed, her cheeks sunken.
"Let me be!... What is it to me?... I shall die!" she muttered, wrenching herself from Marya Dmitrievna's hands with a violent effort and sinking back into her former position.

"Natalie!" said Marya Dmitrievna. "I want what's best for you. Lie still then, stay like that — I won't touch you. But listen. I won't tell you how guilty you are. You know that yourself. But when your father comes back tomorrow, what am I to tell him? Eh?"
Again Natasha's body shook with sobs.
"Suppose he finds out, and your brother, and your fiance?"
"I have no fiance — I've refused him!" cried Natasha.
"That's all the same," continued Marya Dmitrievna. "If they hear of this, will they let it pass? He, your father — I know him — if he challenges him to a duel, will that be all right? Eh?"
"Oh, leave me alone! Why have you interfered at all? Why? Why? Who asked you to?" shouted Natasha, raising herself on the sofa and looking at Marya Dmitrievna with fury.

"But what did you want?" cried Marya Dmitrievna, growing angry again. "Were you kept under lock and key? Who stopped him from coming to the house? Why carry you off as if you were some gypsy dancing girl?... Well, if he had carried you off... do you think they wouldn't have found him? Your father, or brother, or your fiance? And he's a scoundrel, a wretch — that's a fact!"
"He is better than any of you!" exclaimed Natasha, sitting up. "If you hadn't interfered... Oh, my God! What is it all? What is it? Sonya, why?... Go away!"
And she burst into sobs with the despairing intensity with which people mourn disasters they feel they have brought upon themselves. Marya Dmitrievna was about to speak again but Natasha cried out:
"Go away! Go away! You all hate and despise me!" and she threw herself back on the sofa.

Marya Dmitrievna went on lecturing her for some time, insisting that it must all be kept from her father and assuring her that nobody would know anything about it if only Natasha herself would promise to forget it all and not let anyone see that something had happened. Natasha didn't reply, nor did she sob any longer, but she grew cold and had a shivering fit. Marya Dmitrievna put a pillow under her head, covered her with two quilts, and brought her some lime-blossom tea herself, but Natasha didn't respond.
"Well, let her sleep," said Marya Dmitrievna, going out of the room, thinking Natasha had fallen asleep.
But Natasha was not asleep; with a pale face and wide-open eyes she stared straight ahead. All that night she didn't sleep or weep and didn't speak to Sonya, who got up and went to her several times.

The next day Count Rostov returned from his estate near Moscow in time for lunch, as he had promised. He was in very good spirits; the deal with the buyer was going well, and there was nothing to keep him any longer in Moscow, away from the countess whom he missed. Marya Dmitrievna met him and told him that Natasha had been very unwell the day before and that they had sent for the doctor, but that she was better now. Natasha hadn't left her room that morning. With tightly pressed, parched lips and dry, fixed eyes, she sat at the window, restlessly watching the people who drove past and quickly glancing around at anyone who entered the room. She was clearly expecting news of him — that he would come or would write to her.

When the count came to see her, she turned anxiously at the sound of a man's footstep, and then her face resumed its cold and hostile expression. She didn't even get up to greet him. "What is the matter with you, my angel? Are you ill?" asked the count.
After a moment's silence Natasha answered: "Yes, ill."

In reply to the count's anxious questions about why she was so dejected and whether anything had happened to her fiance, she assured him that nothing had happened and asked him not to worry. Marya Dmitrievna confirmed Natasha's assurances that nothing had happened. From the pretense of illness, from his daughter's distress, and from the embarrassed faces of Sonya and Marya Dmitrievna, the count saw clearly that something had gone wrong during his absence, but it was so terrible for him to think that anything disgraceful had happened to his beloved daughter, and he so valued his own cheerful peace of mind, that he avoided further questioning and tried to convince himself that nothing particularly bad had happened; and he was only annoyed that her illness delayed their return to the country.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: From the day his wife arrived in Moscow, Pierre had been intending to go away somewhere, so as not to be near her. Soon after the Rostovs came to Moscow, the effect Natasha had on him made him hurry to carry out his plan. He went to Tver to see Joseph Alexeevich's widow, who had long promised to hand over some papers of her late husband's.

When he returned to Moscow, Pierre was handed a letter from Marya Dmitrievna asking him to come see her on a matter of great importance relating to Andrew Bolkonsky and his fiancee. Pierre had been avoiding Natasha because it seemed to him that his feelings for her were stronger than a married man's should be toward his friend's fiancee. Yet some fate constantly threw them together.

"What can have happened? And what can they want with me?" he thought as he dressed to go to Marya Dmitrievna's. "If only Prince Andrew would hurry up and come and marry her!" he thought on his way there.
On the Tverskoy Boulevard a familiar voice called to him.

"Pierre! Been back long?" someone shouted. Pierre raised his head. In a sleigh drawn by two gray trotting horses that were spattering the dashboard with snow, Anatole and his constant companion Makarin dashed past. Anatole was sitting upright in the classic pose of military dandies, the lower part of his face hidden by his beaver collar and his head slightly tilted. His face was fresh and rosy, his white-plumed hat, tilted to one side, revealed his curled and pomaded hair sprinkled with powdery snow.

"Yes indeed, that's a true sage," thought Pierre. "He sees nothing beyond the pleasure of the moment, nothing troubles him, and so he is always cheerful, satisfied, and serene. What wouldn't I give to be like him!" he thought enviously.
In Marya Dmitrievna's anteroom, the footman who helped him off with his fur coat said that the mistress asked him to come to her bedroom.
When he opened the ballroom door, Pierre saw Natasha sitting at the window with a thin, pale, spiteful face. She glanced around at him, frowned, and left the room with an expression of cold dignity.
"What has happened?" asked Pierre, entering Marya Dmitrievna's room.
"Fine doings!" answered Marya Dmitrievna. "In fifty-eight years I've lived in this world and never known anything so disgraceful!"

And having made him swear not to repeat anything she told him, Marya Dmitrievna informed him that Natasha had refused Prince Andrew without her parents' knowledge, and that the cause of this was Anatole Kuragin, into whose company Pierre's wife had thrown her, and that Natasha had tried to elope with him during her father's absence in order to be secretly married.

Pierre raised his shoulders and listened open-mouthed to what was told him, scarcely able to believe his own ears. That Prince Andrew's deeply loved fiancee — the same Natasha Rostova who used to be so charming — should give up Bolkonsky for that fool Anatole who was already secretly married (as Pierre knew), and should be so in love with him as to agree to run away with him, was something Pierre could not conceive or imagine.

He could not reconcile the charming impression he had of Natasha, whom he had known from childhood, with this new picture of her baseness, folly, and cruelty. He thought of his wife. "They are all alike!" he said to himself, reflecting that he was not the only man unfortunate enough to be tied to a bad woman. But still he pitied Prince Andrew to the point of tears and sympathized with his wounded pride, and the more he pitied his friend the more he thought with contempt and even with disgust of that Natasha who had just passed him in the ballroom with such a look of cold dignity. He didn't know that Natasha's soul was overflowing with despair, shame, and humiliation, and that it was not her fault that her face happened to wear an expression of calm dignity and severity.
"But how could they get married?" said Pierre, in response to Marya Dmitrievna. "He couldn't marry — he's already married!"

"Things get worse by the hour!" exclaimed Marya Dmitrievna. "A fine young man! What a scoundrel! And she's waiting for him — waiting since yesterday. She must be told! Then at least she'll stop expecting him."

After hearing the details of Anatole's marriage from Pierre, and venting her fury against Anatole in a stream of abuse, Marya Dmitrievna told Pierre why she had sent for him. She was afraid that the count or Bolkonsky, who might arrive at any moment, if they found out about this affair (which she hoped to hide from them) might challenge Anatole to a duel, and she therefore asked Pierre to tell his brother-in-law in her name to leave Moscow and not dare let her set eyes on him again. Pierre — only now grasping the danger to the old count, Nicholas, and Prince Andrew — promised to do as she wished. Having briefly and precisely explained what she wanted, she sent him to the drawing room.
"Mind, the count knows nothing. Behave as if you know nothing either," she said. "And I'll go tell her it's no use expecting him! And stay to dinner if you like!" she called after Pierre.
Pierre met the old count, who seemed nervous and upset. That morning Natasha had told him she had refused Bolkonsky.

"Troubles, troubles, my dear fellow!" he said to Pierre. "What troubles one has with these girls without their mother! I do so regret having come here... I'll be frank with you. Have you heard she has broken off her engagement without consulting anyone? It's true this engagement was never much to my liking. Of course he's an excellent man, but still, with his father's disapproval they wouldn't have been happy, and Natasha won't lack for suitors. Still, it's been going on so long, and to take such a step without father's or mother's consent! And now she's ill, and God knows what! It's hard, Count, hard to manage daughters without their mother..."
Pierre saw that the count was very upset and tried to change the subject, but the count kept returning to his troubles.
Sonya entered the room with an agitated face.
"Natasha is not quite well; she's in her room and would like to see you. Marya Dmitrievna is with her and she asks you to come too."
"Yes, you are a great friend of Bolkonsky's — no doubt she wants to send him a message," said the count. "Oh dear! Oh dear! How happy it all was!"
And clutching the sparse gray hair at his temples, the count left the room.

When Marya Dmitrievna told Natasha that Anatole was married, Natasha refused to believe it and insisted on having it confirmed by Pierre himself. Sonya told Pierre this as she led him along the corridor to Natasha's room.

Natasha, pale and stern, was sitting beside Marya Dmitrievna, and her feverishly glistening eyes met Pierre with a questioning look the moment he entered. She didn't smile or nod, but only stared fixedly at him, and her look asked just one thing: was he a friend, or an enemy like the others with regard to Anatole? As for Pierre himself, he clearly didn't exist for her.
"He knows everything," said Marya Dmitrievna, pointing to Pierre and addressing Natasha. "Let him tell you whether I told the truth."
Natasha looked from one to the other like a hunted and wounded animal looking at the approaching dogs and hunters.
"Natalya Ilyinichna," Pierre began, lowering his eyes with a feeling of pity for her and loathing for the thing he had to do, "whether it's true or not should make no difference to you, because..."
"Then it's not true that he's married!"
"Yes, it is true."
"Has he been married long?" she asked. "On your honor?..."
Pierre gave his word of honor.
"Is he still here?" she asked quickly.
"Yes, I just saw him."
She was clearly unable to speak and made a sign with her hands that they should leave her alone.

title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: Pierre drove to Marya Dmitrievna's to tell her that her wish had been fulfilled and Kuragin had been banished from Moscow. The whole house was in a state of alarm and commotion. Natasha was very ill, having — as Marya Dmitrievna told him in secret — poisoned herself the night after she was told Anatole was married, with some arsenic she had secretly obtained. After swallowing a little she had been so frightened that she woke Sonya and told her what she had done. The necessary antidotes had been given in time and she was now out of danger, though still so weak that it was out of the question to move her to the country, and so the countess had been sent for. Pierre saw the distracted count and Sonya's tear-stained face, but couldn't see Natasha.

Pierre dined at the Club that day and heard gossip on all sides about the attempted abduction of Rostova. He firmly denied these rumors, assuring everyone that nothing had happened except that his brother-in-law had proposed to her and been refused. It seemed to Pierre that it was his duty to cover up the whole affair and restore Natasha's reputation.
He was dreading Prince Andrew's return and went every day to the old prince's house for news of him.

Old Prince Bolkonsky had heard all the rumors circulating in the town from Mademoiselle Bourienne and had read the note to Princess Mary in which Natasha had broken off her engagement. He seemed in better spirits than usual and awaited his son with great impatience.
Some days after Anatole's departure, Pierre received a note from Prince Andrew informing him of his arrival and asking him to come and see him.

As soon as he reached Moscow, Prince Andrew had received from his father Natasha's note to Princess Mary breaking off her engagement (Mademoiselle Bourienne had stolen it from Princess Mary and given it to the old prince), and he heard from his father the story of Natasha's elopement attempt, with additions.

Prince Andrew had arrived in the evening, and Pierre came to see him the next morning. Pierre expected to find Prince Andrew in almost the same state as Natasha and was therefore surprised on entering the drawing room to hear him in the study talking loudly and animatedly about some intrigue in Petersburg. The old prince's voice and another occasionally interrupted him. Princess Mary came out to meet Pierre. She sighed, looking toward the door of the room where Prince Andrew was, clearly wanting to express her sympathy with his sorrow, but Pierre saw by her face that she was glad both at what had happened and at the way her brother had taken the news of Natasha's faithlessness.
"He says he expected it," she remarked. "I know his pride won't let him express his feelings, but still he has taken it better, far better, than I expected. Evidently it had to be..."
"But is it possible that it's really all over?" asked Pierre.

Princess Mary looked at him with astonishment. She couldn't understand how he could ask such a question. Pierre went into the study. Prince Andrew, greatly changed and clearly in better health, but with a fresh horizontal wrinkle between his brows, stood in civilian clothes facing his father and Prince Meshchersky, arguing heatedly and gesticulating vigorously. The conversation was about Speransky — the news of whose sudden exile and alleged treachery had just reached Moscow.

"Now he is condemned and blamed by everyone who was enthusiastic about him a month ago," Prince Andrew was saying, "and by those who were unable to understand his aims. To judge a man who is in disgrace and blame him for other men's mistakes is very easy, but I maintain that if anything good has been accomplished in this reign, it was done by him — by him alone."
He paused at the sight of Pierre. His face quivered and immediately assumed a vindictive expression.
"Posterity will do him justice," he concluded, and at once turned to Pierre.
"Well, how are you? Still getting stouter?" he said with energy, but the new wrinkle on his forehead deepened. "Yes, I am well," he said in answer to Pierre's question, and smiled.
To Pierre, that smile clearly said: "I am well, but my health is of no use to anyone now."

After a few words to Pierre about the awful roads from the Polish border, about people he had met in Switzerland who knew Pierre, and about Monsieur Dessalles, whom he had brought from abroad to be his son's tutor, Prince Andrew again joined warmly in the conversation about Speransky that was still going on between the two old men.

"If there were treason, or evidence of secret dealings with Napoleon, they would have been made public," he said with heat and haste. "I do not, and never did, like Speransky personally, but I like justice!"

Pierre now recognized in his friend a need he knew only too well — to get worked up and argue about unrelated matters in order to stifle thoughts that were too painful and too intimate. When Prince Meshchersky had left, Prince Andrew took Pierre's arm and asked him into the room assigned to him. A bed had been made up there, and some open trunks and bags stood about. Prince Andrew went to one and took out a small casket, from which he drew a packet wrapped in paper. He did it all silently and very quickly. He stood up and coughed. His face was gloomy and his lips compressed.
"Forgive me for troubling you..."

Pierre saw that Prince Andrew was going to speak of Natasha, and his broad face expressed pity and sympathy. This expression irritated Prince Andrew, and in a determined, ringing, and unpleasant tone he continued:
"I have received a refusal from Countess Rostova, and have heard reports of your brother-in-law having sought her hand, or something of that kind. Is that true?"
"Both true and untrue," Pierre began; but Prince Andrew interrupted him.
"Here are her letters and her portrait," said he.
He took the packet from the table and handed it to Pierre.
"Give this to the countess... if you see her."
"She is very ill," said Pierre.
"Then she is still here?" said Prince Andrew. "And Prince Kuragin?" he added quickly.
"He left long ago. She has been at death's door."
"I deeply regret her illness," said Prince Andrew; and he smiled like his father — coldly, maliciously, and unpleasantly.
"So Monsieur Kuragin has not honored Countess Rostova with his hand?" said Prince Andrew, and he snorted several times.
"He couldn't marry — he was already married," said Pierre.
Prince Andrew laughed disagreeably, again reminding one of his father.
"And where is your brother-in-law now, if I may ask?" he said.
"He has gone to Peters... But I don't know," said Pierre.
"Well, it doesn't matter," said Prince Andrew. "Tell Countess Rostova that she was and is perfectly free and that I wish her all that is good."
Pierre took the packet. Prince Andrew, as if trying to remember whether he had something more to say, or waiting to see if Pierre would speak, looked steadily at him.
"I say, do you remember our discussion in Petersburg?" asked Pierre, "about..."
"Yes," returned Prince Andrew hastily. "I said that a fallen woman should be forgiven, but I didn't say I could forgive her. I can't."
"But can this be compared...?" said Pierre.

Prince Andrew interrupted him and cried sharply: "Yes, ask for her hand again, be magnanimous, and so on?... Yes, that would be very noble, but I am unable to follow in that gentleman's footsteps. If you wish to be my friend, never speak to me of that... of all that! Well, goodbye. So you'll give her the packet?"
Pierre left the room and went to the old prince and Princess Mary.

The old man seemed livelier than usual. Princess Mary was the same as always, but beneath her sympathy for her brother, Pierre detected her satisfaction that the engagement had been broken off. Looking at them, Pierre realized what contempt and hostility they all felt toward the Rostovs, and that it was impossible in their presence even to mention the name of the woman who could give up Prince Andrew for anyone else.

At dinner the conversation turned to the war, the approach of which was becoming obvious. Prince Andrew talked constantly, arguing now with his father, now with the Swiss tutor Dessalles, and showing an unnatural animation whose cause Pierre understood only too well.

title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: That same evening Pierre went to the Rostovs' to carry out the task entrusted to him. Natasha was in bed, the count was at the Club, and Pierre, after giving the letters to Sonya, went to Marya Dmitrievna, who was eager to know how Prince Andrew had taken the news. Ten minutes later Sonya came to Marya Dmitrievna.
"Natasha insists on seeing Count Bezukhov," said she.
"But how? Shall we take him up to her? The room there hasn't been tidied up."
"No, she has dressed and come to the drawing room," said Sonya.
Marya Dmitrievna only shrugged her shoulders.

"When will her mother get here? She has worried me to death! Now mind, don't tell her everything!" said she to Pierre. "One hasn't the heart to scold her — she's so much to be pitied, so much to be pitied."

Natasha was standing in the middle of the drawing room, thin, with a pale set face, but not at all ashamed as Pierre had expected to find her. When he appeared at the door she grew flustered, clearly unsure whether to go to meet him or to wait.

Pierre hurried to her. He thought she would give him her hand as usual; but she stepped up to him and stopped, breathing heavily, her arms hanging lifelessly, exactly in the pose she used to stand in when she went to the center of the ballroom to sing — but with an entirely different expression on her face.

"Peter Kirilovich," she began rapidly, "Prince Bolkonsky was your friend — is your friend," she corrected herself. (It seemed to her that everything that had once been must now be different.) "He told me once to turn to you..."

Pierre sniffed as he looked at her, but didn't speak. Until now he had reproached her in his heart and tried to despise her, but he now felt so sorry for her that there was no room in his soul for reproach.
"He is here now: tell him... to for... forgive me!" She stopped and breathed still more quickly, but didn't shed tears.
"Yes... I will tell him," answered Pierre; "but..."
He didn't know what to say.
Natasha was clearly dismayed at the thought of what he might think she had meant.
"No, I know all is over," she said hurriedly. "No, that can never be. I'm only tormented by the wrong I've done him. Tell him only that I beg him to forgive, forgive, forgive me for everything..."
She trembled all over and sat down on a chair.
A feeling of pity he had never known before overflowed Pierre's heart.
"I will tell him, I will tell him everything once more," said Pierre. "But... I should like to know one thing..."
"Know what?" Natasha's eyes asked.
"I should like to know — did you love..." Pierre didn't know how to refer to Anatole and flushed at the thought of him — "did you love that bad man?"
"Don't call him bad!" said Natasha. "But I don't know, don't know at all..."
She began to cry, and a still greater sense of pity, tenderness, and love welled up in Pierre. He felt tears trickle under his spectacles and hoped they would not be noticed.
"We won't speak of it anymore, my dear," said Pierre, and his gentle, cordial tone suddenly seemed very strange to Natasha.

"We won't speak of it, my dear — I'll tell him everything; but one thing I beg of you: consider me your friend, and if you want help, advice, or simply to open your heart to someone — not now, but when your mind is clearer — think of me!" He took her hand and kissed it. "I shall be happy if it's in my power..."
Pierre grew confused.
"Don't speak to me like that. I'm not worth it!" exclaimed Natasha, and turned to leave the room, but Pierre held her hand.
He knew he had something more to say to her. But when he said it he was amazed at his own words.
"Stop, stop! You have your whole life before you," he said to her.
"Before me? No! All is over for me," she replied with shame and self-loathing.
"All over?" he repeated. "If I were not myself, but the handsomest, cleverest, and best man in the world, and were free, I would this moment ask on my knees for your hand and your love!"
For the first time in many days, Natasha wept tears of gratitude and tenderness, and glancing at Pierre she went out of the room.

Pierre too, when she had gone, almost ran into the anteroom, holding back tears of tenderness and joy that choked him, and without finding the sleeves of his fur cloak, threw it on and got into his sleigh.
"Where to now, your excellency?" asked the coachman.

"Where to?" Pierre asked himself. "Where can I go now? Surely not to the Club or to pay calls?" All people seemed so pitiful, so poor, compared with the feeling of tenderness and love he was experiencing — compared with that softened, grateful, last look she had given him through her tears.
"Home!" said Pierre, and despite twenty-two degrees of frost, Fahrenheit, he threw open the bearskin cloak from his broad chest and breathed in the air with joy.

It was a clear and frosty night. Above the dirty, poorly lit streets, above the black rooftops, stretched the dark starry sky. Only looking up at the sky did Pierre stop feeling how sordid and humiliating were all earthly things compared with the heights to which his soul had just been raised. At the entrance to Arbat Square an immense expanse of dark starry sky presented itself to his eyes. Almost in the center of it, above the Prechistenka Boulevard, surrounded and sprinkled on all sides by stars but distinguished from them all by its nearness to the earth, its white light, and its long uplifted tail, shone the enormous and brilliant comet of 1812 — the comet said to portend all kinds of disasters and the end of the world. In Pierre, however, that comet with its long luminous tail aroused no feeling of fear. On the contrary, he gazed joyfully, his eyes moist with tears, at this bright comet which, having traveled in its orbit with inconceivable speed through immeasurable space, seemed suddenly — like an arrow piercing the earth — to remain fixed in a chosen spot, vigorously holding its tail erect, shining and displaying its white light among countless other scintillating stars. It seemed to Pierre that this comet fully responded to what was passing in his own softened and uplifted soul, now blossoming into a new life.
